tools.name: License plate readers (ALPR), e.g. Flock Safety cameras
tools.what: Fixed or car-mounted cameras photograph passing license plates and log the plate, time, and place. Police can search past reads to track a car after a crime, or get an alert when a car on a 'hot list' (stolen, wanted, missing person) drives by. With Flock, the agency that owns the cameras decides who can search its data, including other agencies.
tools.common_retention: Flock's default is to delete reads on a rolling 30-day basis, unless a customer's policy or contract says otherwise. In August 2026 Flock urged agencies to cut this to 7 days (a suggestion, not a rule). Arkansas law caps most retention at 150 days.

tools.name: Police body cameras
tools.what: Small cameras worn on an officer's uniform record video and sound of contacts with the public. Each agency's policy says when officers must turn them on, who may watch the video, and when the public can get a copy.
tools.common_retention: Set by state law and agency policy. Texas requires agency policies to keep video at least 90 days. Florida requires recordings to be kept under its public records retention rules.

tools.name: Public cameras and real-time crime centers (RTCC)
tools.what: A real-time crime center is a room inside a police agency where staff watch live feeds and data (cameras, plate readers, 911 calls, records) and pass details like suspect car descriptions to officers on the way to a call. The U.S. Justice Department describes them as central hubs for crime information.
tools.common_retention: Varies by agency; no common standard confirmed.

tools.name: Facial recognition
tools.what: Software compares a face from a photo or video (such as a store camera still) against large photo collections and returns possible matches for an officer to check. A 2023 federal audit found seven federal law enforcement agencies used these services, and six of them ran about 60,000 searches before requiring any training.
tools.common_retention: Not confirmed; depends on the vendor and agency.

tools.name: Gunshot detection (ShotSpotter / SoundThinking)
tools.what: Microphones placed around a neighborhood listen for sounds like gunfire and send police an alert with an estimated location, often before anyone calls 911. Chicago signed a three-year, $33 million contract in 2018.

tools.name: Police drones, including drone-as-first-responder (DFR)
tools.what: Police fly small drones with cameras to look at crime scenes, crashes, searches, and emergencies. In a drone-as-first-responder program, a drone launches to a 911 call and streams video before officers arrive. Chula Vista, California has run one since 2018 and got a federal waiver in 2020 to fly beyond the pilot's line of sight.
tools.common_retention: Not confirmed; Texas and Florida limit when police may use drone images (see states).

tools.name: Doorbell-camera partnerships (Ring and others)
tools.what: Home cameras like Ring record porches and streets. In January 2024 Ring ended the tool that let police ask users for video in its app; police can still use a warrant, and Ring keeps the right to share video without consent in limited emergencies. A planned Ring and Flock Safety link (announced October 2025) was cancelled in February 2026; Ring says it never launched and no customer video went to Flock.
tools.common_retention: Set by the homeowner's own camera plan; not a government record unless shared.

tools.name: Cell-site simulators ("Stingrays")
tools.what: A device that acts like a cell tower so nearby phones connect to it, letting police find or identify a phone. It can briefly disrupt service for other phones nearby. Since 2015, U.S. Justice Department agencies must get a warrant first in most cases, and may not collect calls, texts, or data stored on the phone.
tools.common_retention: Under the 2015 federal policy: delete data once the target phone is found (at least daily), or within 30 days when identifying an unknown phone. Local police rules vary.

tools.name: Social media monitoring software
tools.what: Software that scans, sorts, and saves large numbers of public social media posts by keyword, place, or person. The Brennan Center found local governments spending millions on these tools, and that few had public rules for how they are used.

oversight.tool: Community Control Over Police Surveillance (CCOPS) law
oversight.what: A local law, based on an ACLU model, that lets the city council or county board decide if and how police use surveillance tools, with public input. The ACLU counts 26 places that have adopted one.
oversight.example: Santa Clara County, California (2016), described by the county as the first of its kind in the nation.

src.label: ACLU: Community Control Over Police Surveillance

oversight.tool: Elected-body approval and written use policy before buying
oversight.what: Before a department buys or keeps using a surveillance tool, elected officials must approve a written policy that says its purpose, allowed and banned uses, what data is kept, for how long, and who it is shared with. Officials must weigh benefits against costs, including privacy.
oversight.example: Santa Clara County, California Board of Supervisors (2016).

oversight.what: Each year, departments report in public how each tool was used and what controls are in place, and elected officials review the reports at a public meeting.

Arkansas.summary: License plate readers: Ark. Code Ann. §§ 12-12-1801 to 12-12-1808 bans most uses except by police and a few others (parking, access control, some private property). Plate data may be kept up to 150 days (60 days for private landowners and businesses), longer only while tied to an investigation. Government may not sell, trade, or exchange the data; police may share evidence of a crime with other agencies, and others need a subpoena. Users must compile statistics every six months (plates scanned, matches, arrests) and keep them for 18 months for public review. Arkansas State Police rules limit use to 'legitimate law enforcement purposes', require a log of every disclosure, and send usage reports to the Arkansas Legislative Council quarterly. Body cameras: no statewide requirement to use them was found; a 2025 bill proposed one (final status not confirmed). Local context: in 2026 several Arkansas cities, including Searcy, paused or ended Flock contracts, and Fort Smith cut retention to 7 days.

Texas.summary: License plate readers: NCSL lists no general Texas statute on police ALPR retention or use. Drones: Tex. Gov't Code ch. 423 lists when images may lawfully be captured, including with a warrant, with the owner's consent, in pursuit of a suspect, to document a crime scene, at a death scene or serious crash, to search for a missing person, and in high-risk tactical operations. Images captured in violation cannot be used as evidence. State police agencies, and county and city agencies in places over 150,000 people, must publish a drone-use report every two years (§ 423.008). Body cameras: an agency that uses them must adopt a policy that covers when cameras are on, storage, and public access, and must keep video at least 90 days (Tex. Occ. Code § 1701.655); a 2021 law (the Botham Jean Act, H.B. 929) requires an officer actively in an investigation to keep the camera on.

Florida.summary: License plate readers: Fla. Stat. §§ 316.0777 and 316.0778 make plate images and data with personal information confidential and exempt from public records (they may go to criminal justice agencies and, in some cases, the registered owner), direct the state to set a retention schedule, and bar using them to issue traffic tickets. Drones: Fla. Stat. § 934.50 bars police from using drones to gather evidence except in listed cases, such as with a warrant, to prevent imminent danger or search for a missing person, to watch crowds of 50 or more under a written policy, for traffic management (no tickets from drone images), and at crime or crash scenes; evidence gathered in violation cannot be used in court. Body cameras: not required, but an agency that uses them must have written policies, train staff, review its practices, and keep recordings under state public records rules (Fla. Stat. § 943.1718).
